title: How he came to the trombone and the first Chicago band with Bernie Young
summary: Joe Oliver suggested clarinet but his mother bought a trombone; he studied with William Robinson, formed a band with Bernie Young and the Simeons, joined the union, and learned from Dutrey around Oliver's circle.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: So when was the first music that you were interested in? Did you start on the trombone or which instrument did you start on?

Well, my first instrument was trombone, but it wasn't my favorite instrument. I'd like to tell you, Bill, about how I come to study the trombone. While talking with Joe Oliver, it must have been somewhere around 1920, 1921, somewhere along there. He, I told Joe Oliver that I was going to take lessons on the trombone. So he says, why don't you try the clarinet? The reason Joe suggested to me to take the, take up the clarinet was because I used to whistle so good. And he said people did. So he thought if a fella could whistle like that, he should take up an instrument where he could maneuver, be more nobility. And so before I could make up my mind just what instrument, I came home one evening and in a little green bag, and after seeing the little green bag I became suspicious of it. I went over to bed and I shook a little, a rattle, and in this little green bag when I opened it was a little Carl Fisher trombone. So my mother just about, she's wanted me to play music and she just about made my mind what instrument I should play. Was it a surprise for Christmas or something? Well no it wasn't a Christmas present. It was about in August. Somewhere around 1920 or 21 something like that. So my first teacher was a fella that called Robinson. I think he had a lot to do with my mother buying the trombone. In fact, I learned later that he purchased the trombone from my mother. He was a trombonist. Was that Zoo? No it wasn't Zoo Robinson. This fella's name was William Robinson. He's from here in Chicago. Oh. Yeah, I think he's a Chicagoan. So I'd taken lessons from him about six months or something like that. And nine months I was playing fair for the length of time that I had the trombone and then I went down to Quinn, I was invited down to Quinn Chapel. There was a lady down there who had a little church band, an orchestra. I don't remember my name now. So I stayed around there about four or five months. Was that in Chicago? That was in Chicago. Chicago, yeah. Then I met Simeon boys. Oh yeah. Al Simeon and Omar Simeon and Bernie Young, Snaggs Jones. Met Bernie Young one day. Bernie and I was in the same town, New Orleans, the same neighborhood. Had been knowing Bernie ever since I was big enough to know a man from a bar. And so I didn't know at that time that Bernie was standing a trumpet out of a corner. He had one before he ever came to New Orleans. I saw him in New Orleans with one. But I had forgotten all about that. So we talked things over and he decided he'd get a band together, which he did. So he got Snaggs and Jones who we went to school with in Tarly Farm. Bernie and I went to Tarly Farm school along with Snaggs. Well the Simeon boys they were from New Orleans but they came from down what they called the French part of town. And the fellas who later became the Simeon boys' brother-in-law by the name of Warden played piano. So Bernie got these fellas together and we formed a little band. Then Snaggs left the band and we got Jimmy McEnry on drums. So we played around in the little bands and we weren't in the union at that time and a fella by the name of Monroe was a big fella, about 250 pounds, was the business agent. He just runnin' from one job to another. In fact he ran us right straight into the union. So then we began to play dances out in Gary and down in the Harbour and places like that. After getting in the union sometime we'd have three dates out there sometime the weekend. We were always single and it was more like a picnic then. Music was really more fun now then than it was today rather. So we began to naturally be interested in music. We began to hang around the different spots like the old Rural Garden, Lake and Garden. We met Joe Oliver, Freddie Kebitt, Manny Poiré, so I knew those fellas in New Orleans before I left. And by that time they'd come up here. Joe Oliver was playing at the, it was Dublin at the Dreamling and going down to the Peking. Peking opened one o'clock. Frederick Kebitt and Manny Poiré, they had the band over at the old Rural Garden, later on named the Lincoln Garden. Rob Palmer and Sugar Johnny and Lil Hardin, who later became Mrs. Louis Armstrong, were playing at Deluxe. It was a place right across from the Dreamling, diagonally on the second floor. So we began to make those places and Joe was a great fellow for shooting, playing bass, a pool. So we'd meet every day at 34th and State, there was a place there. And Dutre and Joe and Johnny and Baby, in fact the whole band except Lil, would meet there and we'd ask different questions. And I'd be getting different pointers from Dutre. I used to sit, I sat behind Dutre about four or five consecutive years. And I was very fortunate in having fellas like that to teach me here in Royal Palmer.
